item.title: Shepherds turn to dogs to defend sheep from wolves on the Veluwe
item.description:
Shepherds turn to dogs to defend sheep from wolves on the Veluwe

October 6, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

Shepherds in the Veluwe region have come up with a novel solution to deter wolf attacks by hiring Italian mountain dogs to guard their sheep.

Stichting Schapedrift Ermelo, a volunteer organisation that tends a herd of sheep on the heathlands in Gelderland, acquired two Maremmano-Abruzzese sheepdogs this summer to protect the herd from prowling wolves.

The forested Veluwe region has the biggest concentration of wolves in the Netherlands, with seven packs living in an area of 1,000 square kilometres, since the predators returned in 2019.

The organisation has put up eight-foot electrocuted fences around its sheep enclosure to keep wolves out, but the animals are still vulnerable when they are being herded across the heath.

“We see an increasing threat from wolves,” shepherd Marion Derks told Omroep Gelderland. “And there are a few walking round here that were interested in the sheep.”

The two white-haired dogs have been used for centuries to defend sheep. They are valued for their non-aggressive nature and alertness, Derks said.

“As soon as they see danger, you see their attitude change and they go into defensive mode,” she explained. “They make themselves bigger and more imposing and start barking.”

She said the dogs were not expected to confront or attack wolves. “Their presence is meant to stop the wolves approaching,” Derks explained. “Wolves will take easy prey but if they think it’s going to be too difficult, they’ll look for something else.”

item.title: Dutch woman causes a stir by winning world porridge-making title
item.description:
Dutch woman causes a stir by winning world porridge-making title

October 6, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

When Gina Saarberg started cooking porridge as a student to save money on food, she could never have guessed that it would take her all the way to a world title.

The 28-year-old from Zutphen won the Golden Spurtle at the weekend, the prestigious trophy awarded to the winner of the annual porridge making championships in Carrbridge, Scotland.

Saarberg put her success down to the ingredients she used, including pinhead oats from Noord-Brabant company De Halm and water from her home city in Gelderland. “It’s very soft and I think the mineral content may have something to do with it,” she told BBC Scotland.

A panel of judges headed by former Gleneagles chef Neil Mugg named Saarberg as the best of 30 competitors from 14 countries, including Norway and Australia. She qualified for the event by winning the Dutch national championships in June.

“I started eating porridge in my student days, but I used rolled oats,” she said. “When I switched to oatmeal I found that it made a much creamier porridge – it reminded me of rice pudding.”

The contest, now in its 33rd year, only allows competitors to use oats, water and salt to make traditional porridge, although there is a speciality category where oatmeal can be combined with more exotic ingredients.

Saarberg said: “I only started adding salt to my porridge for the competition and quickly realised that it really brings out the nuances and different aromas, and makes it taste much better.”

The speciality award was won by Australian porridge champion Rob Reid with his porridge cannoli, a fusion of Sicilian and Scottish cuisine based on his own heritage.

“My dad’s Scottish and my mum’s Sicilian, so when I was thinking about what I could do, the idea came to me,” he said. “Then I had to work out how I could possibly make it in 30 minutes.”

item.title: Forbion raises €2.3bn, now Europe’s top biotech investor
item.description:
Forbion raises €2.3bn, now Europe’s top biotech investor

October 6, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

Naarden-based venture capital firm Forbion, which specialises in life sciences companies, has raised €2.3 billion for 2 new biotech funds, its largest fundraising to date.

The firm says it is one of the biggest life sciences venture capital fundraisings in the past 5 years. It takes Forbion’s assets to around €7.5 billion, which it says makes it Europe’s largest specialist life sciences investor, citing data from research firm Preqin.

The funds will finance around 30 companies, ranging from early-stage firms to those already testing drugs on patients.

Forbion says some of the money will go to companies in North America as well as Europe.

Investors include Dutch pension money managers MN and PGGM, as well as US drugmaker Eli Lilly.

The cabinet named life sciences and biotechnology as one of 4 sectors in which it wants to recruit highly skilled foreign workers, under a national talent strategy agreed in July.

item.title: Booking goes to court to force staff to go to the office
item.description:
Booking goes to court to force staff to go to the office

October 6, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

Website Booking.com has asked a court to order its employees to work at least two days a week in the office to settle a long-running internal dispute.

The company’s works council has refused to sign off on a change to its working conditions that would require its 7,000 staff at its head office in Amsterdam to travel in to the capital twice a week.

Booking.com issued guidance at the end of the coronavirus lockdowns in 2022 advising its staff to spend 40% of their working time in the office, but some workers still work almost entirely from home, a spokesman told the Financieele Dagblad.

Any change to working locations needs to be approved by the company’s works council (Ondernemingsraad) under Dutch law, but the council refused to endorse the plan, forcing Booking.com to take the case to court.

The company argues that homeworking is bad for teambuilding and productivity, while staff surveys indicate that most workers find it easier to collaborate with their colleagues when they are in the office.

The new rules would allow staff to choose which days they come in to work: one day to be agreed within members of a team and the other on an individual basis.

The works council has said there is no business case for compelling employees to be present in the office two days a week.

item.title: Cinemas pause Naza screenings ahead of October 7 anniversary
item.description:
Cinemas pause Naza screenings ahead of October 7 anniversary

October 6, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

Cinema screenings of the Israeli documentary Naza, which investigates the war on Gaza, is being suspended from most Dutch cinemas from Tuesday until the weekend so that they do not coincide with the commemoration of the October 7 Hamas attacks.

This is in line with the wishes of the film’s makers, two Israeli documentarians, who fear that their safety – and that of their families, who are still in Israel – will be further threatened if the film is shown around the date.

The Dutch film distributor Cherry Pickers, which is responsible for the film in the Netherlands, has said it will heed their wishes. The duo have not yet returned to Israel since the film’s release, but their families have been harassed and the government is moving to strip them of their nationality.

Naza is composed of interviews with 24 anonymous Israeli intelligence and military personnel involved in military campaign on Gaza since October 7, 2023. They describe how civilians were routinely killed, often hundreds at a time, to target single militants.

They also describe how surveillance was used to track suspects and wait until they were at home with their families before bombing them, as well as using special AI systems to select and kill targets. Israeli officials have disputed many of the claims.

A screening of the film in Delft last week on the opening day was interrupted by an Israeli group, one of whom took a microphone and began telling the audience how her family was murdered by Hamas. Another tried to project footage of the attacks onto the cinema screen.

item.title: Patients fear shortage of medicinal cannabis when rules change
item.description:
Patients fear shortage of medicinal cannabis when rules change

October 6, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

Patients who rely on medicinal cannabis are worried about supplies running out when the government ends its contract with the only Dutch licensed grower next year.

The health ministry is not renewing the contract between the Bureau for Medicinal Cannabis (BMC) and Bedrocan from 2027 as part of a plan to liberalise the supply chain by letting suppliers sell directly to pharmacies.

But the rule changes have been delayed, meaning that Bedrocan, based in Emmeloord, will be unable to sell its products at all from next year.

The government says it will import medicinal cannabis from abroad to ensure patients are not denied treatment. The BMC has ordered in extra stocks for the start of next year, but these medicines will go out of date in mid-2027.

Around 7,000 people in the Netherlands are prescribed cannabis for conditions such as MS and epilepsy, or as a form of palliative care.

The MS Vereniging, which represents people with multiple sclerosis, warned that using a different variant of the medicine would be less effective for some patients.

Specific variety

In a letter to health minister Sophie Hermans, the MS association said some patients who had been prescribed cannabis long-term were dependent on a “specific variety” of the drug and switching to an alternative version would affect the quality of their treatment.

The ministry disputed this in its reply, saying there was “no scientific evidence that different varieties have different therapeutic effects”.

But Renger Witkamp, professor of pharmacology at Wageningen University, said different varieties of cannabis were known to work differently. “Cannabis is different from synthetic medicines,” he told the Volkskrant. “The plant contains dozens of chemicals that collectively determine the effect.

“The relationship between those chemicals is determined by the plant variety, but also by the conditions in which it is grown, such as light, soil and fertiliser.”

item.title: Heinen struggling to hit deadline for capital gains tax reform
item.description:
Heinen struggling to hit deadline for capital gains tax reform

October 6, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

Finance minister Eelco Heinen is in a race against time to introduce a new capital gains tax system by his promised deadline of 2028, financial institutions have warned.

Heinen is under pressure from right-wing opposition parties JA21 and SGP to replace the current income tax regime as quickly as possible as part of the deal to pass next year’s budget.

The minister also needs to plug a €7 billion hole in the finances after left-wing parties Pro and Volt forced the government to drop its planned cuts to social security as the price for their support. The minority government needs the votes of at least two opposition parties in parliament to pass legislation.

Heinen said 2028 could be achieved with “the maximum stretch from everyone”. But banks and the Council of State, which advises the cabinet on the legal implications of its bills, cast doubt on his timetable when asked by NOS.

The Council of State said it was “impossible” to have its analysis ready by next Monday, October 12, so that parliament can debate the bill next week. A spokesman said October 19 was the earliest realistic date.

The Dutch banking association NVB said its members need time to adapt their IT systems so they can pass the relevant details of their customers’ income to the tax office.

Risk of fraud

If customers have to provide the information themselves it increases the risk of delays, inaccuracies and fraud, the banks have warned.

The tax office is also under pressure to update its systems to deal with other reforms, such as the introduction of compulsory work incapacity insurance for people who are self-employed.

Changing the income tax method at the same time would be likely to delay the insurance plan by a year, civil servants told NOS.

Every year that the cabinet delays the overhaul of the income tax system is costing the government an estimated €3.5 billion in lost revenue.

Assumed gains

Heinen’s latest draft does not explain how he plans to compensate for the income lost during the transition to capital gains tax, which will only raise tax on assets and investments when they are sold.

The current “box 3” method charges taxpayers on their assumed gains from their assets every year, but the Supreme Court struck out this system in 2021 because it was unfair on savers whose wealth was held in low-interest accounts.

Heinen included a proposal to lower the thresholds for the “box 3” wealth tax as a stopgap measure in his submission to the Council of State, but parliament has already indicated it does not support this reform.

item.title: Unhealthy food outlets dominate Dutch cities, say researchers
item.description:
Unhealthy food outlets dominate Dutch cities, say researchers

October 6, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

The food in 10 major Dutch cities has become less healthy over the past decade, according to new research by Amsterdam UMC.

Health executives from the 10 cities have written to health minister Sophie Hermans urging her to speed up a promised food law that would let councils limit unhealthy outlets, Het Parool reported on Tuesday.

The researchers scored 31 types of food outlet, from greengrocers to fast-food chains. The scores combined expert ratings with checks of more than 83,000 products against the “Wheel of Five” (Schijf van Vijf), the official Dutch healthy eating guidelines.

Each neighbourhood was then given a score from -500 (extremely unhealthy) to +500 (extremely healthy), based on the type, number and proximity of nearby outlets.

All 10 cities scored negative in both 2014 and 2024, ranging from -252 in Groningen to -327 in Leiden. Amsterdam fell from -287 to -301. Across the cities, 77% of neighbourhoods scored lower in 2024 than 10 years earlier.

In Amsterdam, 96% of food outlets fall into categories the researchers rate as unhealthy. Some 87 of the city’s 90 secondary schools and vocational colleges are in what the report calls a “very unhealthy” food environment.

The councils say they currently lack a clear legal basis to refuse outlets selling unhealthy food.

“That more than nine in 10 secondary schools and vocational colleges are in an unhealthy food environment means young people are surrounded every day by an offer that makes choosing healthily harder,” Amsterdam health executive Alexander Scholtes told Het Parool. “I am not willing to resign myself to that.”

item.title: Cabinet wants phones out of schools from January
item.description:
Cabinet wants phones out of schools from January

October 5, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

The cabinet is calling on all primary and secondary schools to ban mobile phone use starting from January.

In a new proposal from digital economy minister Willemijn Aerdts, children would not be allowed to use their phones on school grounds, rules about children appearing in family vlogs would be tightened and the time children spend scrolling would be limited.

“Online, on social media or in video games, children quickly become exposed and face unacceptable risks,” Aerdts said in the proposal, called ‘Strategy Letter on Children’s Rights’.

Since 2024, there have been national agreements prohibiting the use of phones in the classroom.

The government does not have the authority to order schools to implement the policy and the education ministry will work with schools to come up with an agreement.

Aerdts is also keen to limit how children are used in online content, like family-style YouTube.

The cabinet also intends on commissioning research into sites like Netflix, YouTube, Roblox, Fortnite, ChatGPT, Instagram, Snapchat, and TikTok and their impact on children.

Earlier this year, the government has backed an EU-wide minimum age for social media. D66, VVD and CDA agreed in their coalition agreement to push for an enforceable European minimum age of 15.

item.title: Nine Dutch restaurants win first Michelin stars
item.description:
Nine Dutch restaurants win first Michelin stars

October 5, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

Nine Dutch restaurants have won Michelin stars for the first time in the 2026 edition of the guide, and two of them went straight in with two stars.

Azurite in Delft, run by chef Mario Ridder, and Suis in Schin op Geul, near Valkenburg, both entered the guide at two-star level, broadcaster NOS reported.

Suis only opened at the end of April, after chef Ralf Berendsen left La Butte aux Bois to start his own restaurant.

The 7 new one-star restaurants are spread across the country: Nassau in Groningen, Le Epifaan in Veeningen in Drenthe, Wild Atelier at the De Echoput hotel in Hoog Soeren, Bij Sidney in Loenen aan de Vecht, De Cuijt in Mierlo near Eindhoven, Rozewied in Kortgene in Zeeland, and Ambrozijn in Valkenburg.

Le Epifaan is run by Jarno Eggen, who previously cooked at two-star De Groene Lantaarn in Staphorst before it closed. Rozewied’s chefs, Noëmie Haentjens and Ferdy van Rijswijk, also won Michelin’s Young Chef Award.

Matthijs Vrancken and Nouri Haj Romdhane of Brut172 in Reijmerstok won the sommelier award. Château Neercanne in Maastricht won the award for service.

De Librije in Zwolle remains the only three-star restaurant in the Netherlands, a rating it has held since 2004. Nelson Tanate now leads the kitchen following the death of co-owner and chef Jonnie Boer in April 2025.

No Amsterdam restaurant won a new star this year, and Daalder and De Juwelier lost theirs, AT5 reported.

In total, the Netherlands has 119 starred restaurants, the same number as last year.
